title: Princely states of India
summary: When the British Crown took over from the East India Company in 1858, it did not rule all of India directly. About two-fifths of the subcontinent stayed under Indian princes: maharajas, nawabs, the Nizam of Hyderabad and hundreds of minor chiefs. Many of their states had signed 'subsidiary alliances' with the Company, giving up control of foreign affairs and accepting British troops in return for protection. After 1858 the Crown inherited these treaties and claimed 'paramountcy': the rulers ran their own internal affairs, but Britain controlled their defence and foreign relations, kept a Resident or Political Agent at their courts, and could depose a ruler for misrule. In 1947 there were 565 recognised states, from Hyderabad and Kashmir, each larger than many European countries, to estates of a few villages. When British rule ended, paramountcy lapsed and each ruler was asked to join India or Pakistan. Most signed Instruments of Accession by 15 August 1947. Junagadh's Nawab chose Pakistan, but India took over in November 1947; Kashmir's Maharaja acceded to India in October 1947 during a tribal invasion; Kalat joined Pakistan in March 1948; and Hyderabad was taken over by the Indian Army in September 1948. These outlines are traced from the Imperial Gazetteer of India maps of 1909 and from OpenHistoricalMap. The largest states are drawn singly; the hundreds of small ones are grouped by agency. Boundaries are approximate, and they show the states as they were around 1909.

regions.name: Hyderabad
regions.note: The Nizam's state in the Deccan, one of the two largest princely states with Jammu and Kashmir. The Nizam did not accede in 1947; the Indian Army took control between 13 and 18 September 1948 (Operation Polo). Outline from OpenHistoricalMap, matching the 1909 Imperial Gazetteer map; Berar is shown separately. Drawn area c. 213,900 km².

regions.name: Berar (Hyderabad Assigned Districts)
regions.note: Assigned by the Nizam to East India Company administration under an 1853 treaty, so it was Hyderabad's territory but British-run. Leased permanently to the British on 5 November 1902 and joined to the Central Provinces from 1 October 1903. Drawn area c. 43,600 km².

regions.name: Mysore (under British commission)
regions.capital: Mysore (Bangalore was the seat of the British commission 1831–1881)
regions.note: The British took over direct administration of Mysore in 1831. The state kept its identity and was handed back (the 'rendition') in 1881 to Chamarajendra Wadiyar X. Drawn area c. 79,600 km².

regions.name: Mysore
regions.note: Ruled again by the Wodeyar dynasty after the 1881 rendition; one of the largest states in the south. Joined the Indian Union on 9 August 1947. Drawn area c. 79,600 km².

regions.name: Jammu and Kashmir
regions.note: Ruled by the Dogra maharajas, including Ladakh and the Gilgit region (the outline follows OpenHistoricalMap and includes claimed frontier areas). Maharaja Hari Singh signed the Instrument of Accession to India dated 26 October 1947; Mountbatten accepted it on 27 October. Drawn area c. 186,200 km².

regions.name: Cochin
regions.note: Small kingdom north of Travancore, around Ernakulam and Trichur. It acceded to India in 1947 and merged with Travancore on 1 July 1949. Its boundary with Travancore is approximate (traced from the 1909 Madras map). Drawn area c. 3,100 km².

regions.name: Travancore
regions.note: Southern kingdom on the Malabar coast. Its ruler agreed to accede to India on 12 August 1947; it merged with Cochin on 1 July 1949. Outline from OpenHistoricalMap, with the Cochin part cut off along the 1909 map's boundary (approximate). Drawn area c. 20,000 km².

regions.name: Cutch
regions.note: Peninsula state ruled by the Rao; the outline includes the Great Rann. Acceded to India in 1947. Drawn area c. 42,200 km².

regions.name: Kolhapur
regions.note: Maratha state of the Bhonsle line of Shivaji, the chief state of the Kolhapur and Southern Maratha Country agency. Outline from OpenHistoricalMap. Acceded to India in 1947. Drawn area c. 7,700 km².

regions.name: Sikkim
regions.note: Himalayan kingdom, a British protectorate from the 1861 Treaty of Tumlong. It did not join India in 1947; it became an Indian protectorate in 1950 and an Indian state in 1975. Drawn area c. 7,100 km².

regions.name: Manipur
regions.note: Hill kingdom on the Burma frontier. Acceded to India on 11 August 1947. Drawn area c. 22,400 km².

regions.name: Hill Tippera (Tripura)
regions.note: Kingdom east of Bengal, called Hill Tippera in British records. Acceded to India on 13 August 1947. Drawn area c. 10,500 km².

regions.name: Bahawalpur
regions.note: Muslim-ruled state on the Sutlej, south-west of the Punjab. The Nawab signed accession to Pakistan on 5 October 1947, accepted on 9 October; the first state to accede to Pakistan. Drawn area c. 45,000 km².

regions.name: Khairpur
regions.note: State of the Talpur Mirs in Sind. Acceded to Pakistan on 3 October 1947. Drawn area c. 16,200 km².

regions.name: Kalat (with Kharan, Las Bela and Makran)
regions.note: The Khan of Kalat headed a confederacy of Baloch chiefs; Kharan, Las Bela and Makran are included in this outline (Kharan was separated from Kalat as its own state in the 1930s). Kharan, Las Bela and Makran acceded to Pakistan first; Kalat acceded on 27 March 1948. Kalat, Kharan and Las Bela outlines are from OpenHistoricalMap; Makran is traced from the 1909 map. Drawn area c. 191,500 km².

regions.name: Chitral
regions.note: Mountain state of the Mehtar, allied with the British from 1885 (agreement of 1891). The Mehtar signed the Instrument of Accession to Pakistan on 6 November 1947. The outline is hand-drawn from the 1909 North-West Frontier Province map and is larger than the 14,860 km² given for 1951. Drawn area c. 19,000 km².

regions.name: Bikaner
regions.note: Rathore state in the Thar Desert, in the Rajputana Agency. Acceded to India in 1947. Drawn area c. 59,100 km².

regions.name: Jaisalmer
regions.note: Bhati Rajput desert state in the Rajputana Agency. Acceded to India in 1947. Drawn area c. 40,000 km².

regions.name: Jodhpur (Marwar)
regions.note: The largest state in Rajputana, ruled by Rathores. Acceded to India in August 1947. Drawn area c. 92,400 km².

regions.name: Jaipur
regions.note: Kachhwaha state, including the Shekhawati chiefships. Acceded to India in 1947. Drawn area c. 34,400 km².

regions.name: Udaipur (Mewar)
regions.note: Senior Rajput house (Sisodias) in the Aravalli hills. The small state of Shahpura sits inside this outline. Acceded to India in 1947. Drawn area c. 32,600 km².

regions.name: Kotah (with Jhalawar)
regions.note: Kotah and Jhalawar (carved out of Kotah) formed the Kotah and Jhalawar Agency; they are drawn together because their boundary cannot be read reliably on the 1909 map. Acceded to India in 1947. Drawn area c. 17,500 km².

regions.name: Gwalior
regions.note: Maratha state of the Scindias. This outline is the main northern block (Gwalior, Bhind, Sheopur, Narwar, Isagarh); Gwalior's Malwa districts (Ujjain, Mandsaur, Shajapur and others) are interleaved with other states and are inside the Central India group. Acceded to India in 1947. Drawn area c. 33,600 km².

regions.name: Indore
regions.note: Maratha state of the Holkars. Outline is the main Indore–Nimar block; detached parts (such as Rampura-Bhanpura) are inside the Central India group. Its edges are approximate. Acceded to India in 1947. Drawn area c. 12,500 km².

regions.name: Bhopal
regions.note: Muslim-ruled state, for much of the 19th century governed by begums. Its edges are approximate. Shown until 1947 with the other Central India states. Drawn area c. 14,800 km².

regions.name: Rewa
regions.note: The largest state in Baghelkhand. Acceded to India in 1947. Drawn area c. 34,400 km².

title: South Asian kingdoms to 1000 CE
summary: Kingdoms of South Asia before 1000 CE that the base border data leaves out: the Western Gangas of Karnataka, the Licchavis of Nepal, Zhangzhung in Western Tibet, the Hindu Shahis, the kingdoms of Sindh and Multan, the Vishnukundinas and Eastern Chalukyas of Andhra, the Kalachuris, the Chera Perumals, the dynasties of Odisha and Dakshina Kosala, the Later Guptas, the Ikshvakus of Vijayapuri and Porus. Extents are approximate reconstructions from regional descriptions in the sources, trimmed to stay clear of the states the atlas already draws.

regions.name: Western Ganga kingdom (Gangavadi)
regions.capital: Kolar (Kuvalala), then Talakad (Talakadu) on the Kaveri from c. 390
regions.note: Gangavadi: the modern Mysore, Hassan, Mandya, Ramanagara, Chamarajanagar, Tumkur, Kolar and Bangalore districts (Wikipedia). Before c. 470 only the eastern districts round Kolar and Talakad are drawn; Sendraka (Chikkamagaluru, Belur), Punnata and the northern Kongu country were added by c. 470, and Kongu was held, contested with the Pandyas, into the 9th century. The Gangas were feudatories of the Badami Chalukyas (6th–8th c.) and, after a century of resistance, allies of the Rashtrakutas; they are drawn as their own kingdom throughout. The Tungabhadra lands granted after Takkolam (949) are not drawn. Ended when the Cholas took Gangavadi c. 1000. Drawn from a hand-traced extent, then cut back wherever the atlas's Cliopatria borders already place another state in the same years, so the shape shrinks or vanishes when that layer claims the area.

title: South Asian kingdoms, 1550–1857
summary: From the fall of Vijayanagara's capital to the Revolt of 1857, the map's border data (Cliopatria) draws the Mughal, Maratha, Durrani and British realms and a few successor states, but leaves out many kingdoms that ruled themselves. This layer adds them. In the south: Travancore, Cochin, the Zamorin's Calicut, the Keladi Nayakas, the last Aravidu kings of Vijayanagara, the Nayaks of Gingee, and Mysore redrawn through the Wodeyar, Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan periods. In the Deccan and centre: the Gond kingdoms of Garha-Mandla, Deogarh and Chanda, Bastar, Ratanpur, Hyderabad after 1799, Nagpur, Satara, and the Holkar, Scindia and Gaekwad states after 1818. In the north: the Rajput kingdoms and Jat Bharatpur after the Mughal collapse, Rohilkhand, the reduced Awadh of 1803–56, Kumaon, Garhwal, Ladakh and Sikkim. In the east: the Ahom, Koch, Kachari, Jaintia, Manipur and Tripura kingdoms. In the west: Kutch and the Khanate of Kalat. Outlines are traced from the Imperial Gazetteer Atlas historical plates (1765, 1805, 1837, 1857) where those show a state, and otherwise reconstructed from rivers, hill lines and the later princely-state borders; they are approximate. States that continued as princely states end in 1857, where the princely-states layer begins.

regions.name: Venad (early Travancore)
regions.note: Venad, the kingdom from which Travancore grew, held the south-western tip of India: Thiruvananthapuram and Kanyakumari, with Attingal. Kollam (Desinganad), Kayamkulam and the lands further north were separate chiefdoms. Its 16th–17th century rulers are poorly documented; the outline follows the Wikipedia description of Venad's core districts, and the northern edge near Varkala is a convention. Sibling layers may draw Venad before 1550.

regions.name: Travancore under Marthanda Varma
regions.note: Marthanda Varma (r. 1729–1758) turned Venad into Travancore: he annexed Attingal, Kollam/Desinganad (1742) and Kayamkulam (1746) and beat the Dutch at Colachel (1741). One outline is drawn for this whole phase of conquest, with its northern edge just beyond Kayamkulam, so the 1730s are drawn somewhat too large.

regions.name: Kingdom of Travancore
regions.note: After taking Ambalappuzha, Thekkumkur and Vadakkumkur (1749–54; Treaty of Mavelikkara with Cochin, 1753), Travancore reached roughly the extent it kept until 1949. Plates 28 and 29 of the Imperial Gazetteer Atlas show it this way in 1765, 1805, 1837 and 1857. It accepted a subsidiary alliance with the East India Company (1795, 1805). Drawn here to 1857; the princely-states layer takes over in 1858. The border with Cochin around Kochi was a patchwork of enclaves and is simplified here.

regions.name: Kingdom of Cochin
regions.note: Cochin was a Portuguese ally (1503–1663) and then a Dutch protectorate (1663–1795). The Zamorin occupied its northern districts in 1756–62, Mysore exacted tribute from 1774, and it became a British subsidiary state in 1791/1809. The outline follows the Cochin State of plates 28–29 (1805–1857), which matches the 1909 state. Its 16th–17th-century borders with the Zamorin and with the Travancore chiefdoms moved often and are not drawn. Drawn to 1857; the princely-states layer covers 1858 onwards.

regions.name: Kingdom of Calicut (the Zamorin)

rulers.name: Manavikraman (various Zamorins of the same title)
Zamorin allied with the Dutch against the Portuguese
Zamorin who burned his palace as Hyder Ali arrived

regions.note: The Zamorins held south Malabar, from the Korapuzha river south to Chettuva, inland through Ernad and Nilambur, and fought Portugal and Cochin for a century. Palakkad (Palghat) under its own raja, and the northern Kolathiri lands, are outside the outline. Hyder Ali conquered Calicut in 1766. Zamorins took personal names that are rarely recorded, so the rulers listed are by event. The inland edge is approximate.

regions.name: Keladi Nayakas (Ikkeri / Bednur)
regions.note: The Keladi Nayakas were Vijayanagara governors who became independent after Talikota (1565). They held Shimoga and Chikmagalur on the plateau and the Canara coast from about Kasaragod to Honnavar. Shivappa Nayaka drove the Portuguese from the Canara ports. Hyder Ali took Bidanur in 1763. The northern edge (Sonda, Banavasi) and the line against Mysore and Coorg are approximate.

regions.name: Kingdom of Mysore (Wodeyar principality)
regions.note: This is the small Wodeyar principality around Mysore while it was a Vijayanagara feudatory. Raja Wodeyar took Srirangapatna from the Vijayanagara viceroy in 1610. In this period the layer replaces the map's Cliopatria 'Kingdom of Mysore' polygons with its own outlines (1572–1857).

regions.name: Kingdom of Mysore (Srirangapatna)
regions.note: After taking Srirangapatna in 1610, the Wodeyars expanded over Mandya, southern Hassan, Chamarajanagar and the Kaveri country under Raja Wodeyar and Kanthirava Narasaraja I. The edges are approximate.

regions.name: Kingdom of Mysore under Chikka Devaraja and successors
regions.note: Chikka Devaraja Wodeyar (r. 1673–1704) brought Mysore close to its later core: Hassan, Tumkur and Bangalore (bought from the Mughals in 1689), with Baramahal and Salem on the eastern edge. The outline follows the Cliopatria extent for 1673–1798 with Coorg and Keladi left out. From 1734 the Dalavayi brothers, and from 1761 Hyder Ali, held real power.

regions.name: Mysore under Hyder Ali (with Bednur)
regions.note: Hyder Ali took Bidanur (the Keladi kingdom) and the Canara coast in 1763 and Sonda in 1764. Sira was also taken in the 1760s, but its exact extent is not drawn.

regions.name: Mysore under Hyder Ali (with Malabar)
regions.note: Hyder conquered Malabar in 1766 (Calicut, the Kolathiri lands, Palakkad), Coorg in 1773, and held Coimbatore, Dindigul and Baramahal. Cochin paid tribute but is drawn separately; Travancore stayed independent. Chitradurga (taken 1779) lies outside this outline.

regions.name: Mysore under Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan
regions.note: The kingdom was at its largest after Hyder took Bellary and Gooty (1775–76) and Chitradurga, Cuddapah and the Savanur country (1776–79). The Treaty of Gajendragad (1787) returned some northern districts to the Marathas. The northern edge is a mainstream simplification along the Tungabhadra and Krishna watershed. Plate 28 (1765) and contemporary accounts were used to check it.

regions.name: Mysore under Tipu Sultan after the Treaty of Seringapatam
regions.note: The Treaty of Seringapatam (1792) took half of Tipu's lands. Malabar, Coorg, Dindigul and Salem–Baramahal went to the Company, and the lands north of the Tungabhadra to the Nizam and the Marathas. Tipu kept the plateau, Coimbatore and Canara. He died when Srirangapatna fell on 4 May 1799. Whether Wayanad stayed with Mysore is disputed; it is left out here.

regions.name: Kingdom of Mysore (restored Wodeyars)
regions.note: In 1799 the Company restored the Wodeyars to a reduced, landlocked Mysore that matches the princely state of plate 29 (1837, 1857) and of 1909. The Company ran it directly through a commission from 1831 to 1881. Drawn to 1857; the princely-states layer covers 1858 onwards.

regions.name: Vijayanagara Empire (Aravidu dynasty, Penukonda and Chandragiri)
regions.note: After Talikota (1565) and the sack of Hampi, the Aravidu kings ruled from Penukonda and then Chandragiri. They still held Anantapur, Chittoor, Kolar and the Vellore country and claimed overlordship of the Nayaks of Madurai, Thanjavur and Gingee and of Mysore. The map's Cliopatria 'Vijayanagara Empire' stops in 1571, so these last decades were blank. Only lands under direct Aravidu rule are drawn. Their northern and eastern edges against Golconda and Bijapur moved often and are approximate.

regions.name: Vijayanagara Empire (Aravidu dynasty, Chandragiri and Vellore)
regions.note: The civil war after Venkatapati Raya's death (Battle of Toppur, 1616), followed by Golconda's and Bijapur's advance into the Carnatic, reduced the empire to the Chandragiri–Vellore country. Vellore fell around 1646, which is taken as the empire's end (Wikipedia: 1336–1646); Sriranga III lived on in exile until 1678. The outline is approximate.

regions.name: Nayaks of Gingee
regions.note: Gingee was one of the three Tamil Nayakships under Vijayanagara, alongside Madurai and Thanjavur (both drawn on the map). It held the land between the Palar and the Kollidam (Coleroon) until Bijapur took the fort in 1649. It is drawn from 1572 only, because the map draws it inside the Vijayanagara Empire before then. Its line with the Aravidu territory to the north and with Thanjavur to the south is approximate.

regions.name: Hyderabad State (the Nizam's dominions)
regions.note: The map's Cliopatria Hyderabad stops in 1798. The Nizam entered a subsidiary alliance in 1798 and in 1800 ceded his share of the Mysore conquests (the 'Ceded Districts': Bellary, Cuddapah and others). From then on the state matched the Nizam's dominions of plate 28 (1805), plate 29 (1837, 1857) and 1909. Berar was then still under the Bhonsles of Nagpur.

regions.name: Hyderabad State (with Berar)
regions.note: The Treaty of Deogaon (1803) gave the Nizam Berar west of the Wardha river, which is drawn as part of Hyderabad. Plate 29 (1837) colours Berar with the Nizam's lands. In 1853 Berar was 'assigned' to the Company to pay for the Hyderabad Contingent.

regions.name: Hyderabad State (Berar assigned)
regions.note: After the Treaty of 1853 assigned Berar to the Company, plate 29 (1857) still shades it with the Nizam's lands (formal sovereignty stayed with the Nizam). Here it is left out, because the Company administered it. Drawn to 1857; the princely-states layer covers 1858 onwards.

regions.name: Kingdom of Nagpur (Bhonsle)
regions.note: After the Third Anglo-Maratha War (Sitabuldi, 1817) the Bhonsles lost the Saugor and Narmada territories and kept Nagpur, Wardha (east of the river), Chanda, Bhandara, Chhindwara and Chhattisgarh as a protected state. The Company annexed it by lapse in 1853. Plate 29 (1837, 'Bhonsla') shows this extent. Before 1818 the Bhonsle lands are part of the map's Maratha Empire. Bastar and the other feudatory chiefdoms are left out.

regions.name: Satara State (Bhonsle rump)
regions.note: After the Peshwa's fall the Company set up Shivaji's descendant Pratap Singh in a small state around Satara. It was annexed by lapse in 1848–49. The outline is approximate.

regions.name: Indore State (Holkar)
regions.note: After Mahidpur (1817) and the Treaty of Mandsaur (1818), Holkar's state was reduced to scattered districts under British protection. Drawn here are its Indore–Nimar core and (as a separate region) the Rampura–Bhanpura district; smaller enclaves are left out. Before 1818 Holkar's lands are part of the map's Maratha Empire.

regions.name: Indore State (Rampura–Bhanpura)
regions.note: This is Holkar's northern district around Rampura and Bhanpura, between Mewar, Kota and Scindia's Malwa lands. The edges are approximate.

regions.name: Gwalior State (Scindia)
regions.note: The map draws Scindia's state from 1820 to 1845 (as a relabelled Cliopatria polygon), but nothing from 1846. This outline continues the northern block of that polygon (Gwalior, Narwar, Guna, Bhind) to 1857. It is unchanged by the Gwalior campaign of 1843 (Maharajpur, Panniar), which brought a British-officered contingent but little loss of land.

regions.name: Gwalior State (Scindia's Malwa districts)
regions.note: Scindia's Malwa districts around Ujjain, Shajapur and Mandsaur, drawn approximately without Holkar's and the small Rajput states' enclaves.

regions.name: Baroda State (Gaekwad; Baroda district)
regions.note: From 1802 the Gaekwads were allied with the Company, and after 1818 their state, scattered across Gujarat, was a protected state. Only the two largest blocks are drawn: the Baroda district here and the Kadi district separately. Navsari and Amreli are left out. Before 1818 Gujarat is drawn inside the map's Maratha Empire.

regions.name: Baroda State (Gaekwad; Kadi district)
regions.note: The Gaekwads' northern district around Kadi and Patan. The outline is approximate.

regions.name: Cutch (Kingdom of Kutch)
regions.note: The Jadeja Raos ruled Kutch and the Rann from Bhuj, founded in 1549. They paid tribute to the Mughals from the 1590s while ruling themselves, and came under British protection in 1819. The map draws Kutch inside the Mughal Empire (to 1751) and then leaves it blank, so it is drawn here as its own kingdom throughout. Plates 28 and 29 show 'Cutch' with this extent. The northern edge across the Rann is a convention. Drawn to 1857; the princely-states layer covers 1858 onwards.

regions.name: Kingdom of Mewar (Udaipur)
regions.note: Mewar was the one major Rajput kingdom that refused Mughal suzerainty. Akbar took Chittor in 1568, and Pratap fought at Haldighati (1576) and later won back most of the hill country; Amar Singh I submitted by treaty in 1615. The map draws Mewar inside the Mughal Empire from 1564, so this region overlaps that outline. The extent is its 1909 territory, with Chittor (lost 1568) included throughout; this is approximate.

regions.name: Kingdom of Mewar (Udaipur State)
regions.note: From 1752 the map's Mughal outline no longer covers Rajputana, so the Rajput states, which had been Mughal vassal kingdoms and are drawn inside the Mughal Empire before then, are drawn here as states. Maratha (Scindia, Holkar) armies took tribute and districts until the treaties of 1817–18 put them under British protection. The borders follow the 1909 Rajputana states, which changed little after 1818; before 1818 parts were held by Maratha chiefs (Ajmer by Scindia, 1756–1818), and this is not drawn. Drawn to 1857; the princely-states layer covers 1858 onwards.

regions.name: Kingdom of Marwar (Jodhpur)
regions.note: From 1752 the map's Mughal outline no longer covers Rajputana, so the Rajput states, which had been Mughal vassal kingdoms and are drawn inside the Mughal Empire before then, are drawn here as states. Maratha (Scindia, Holkar) armies took tribute and districts until the treaties of 1817–18 put them under British protection. The borders follow the 1909 Rajputana states, which changed little after 1818; before 1818 parts were held by Maratha chiefs (Ajmer by Scindia, 1756–1818), and this is not drawn. Drawn to 1857; the princely-states layer covers 1858 onwards.

regions.name: Kingdom of Amber (Jaipur)
regions.note: From 1752 the map's Mughal outline no longer covers Rajputana, so the Rajput states, which had been Mughal vassal kingdoms and are drawn inside the Mughal Empire before then, are drawn here as states. Maratha (Scindia, Holkar) armies took tribute and districts until the treaties of 1817–18 put them under British protection. The borders follow the 1909 Rajputana states, which changed little after 1818; before 1818 parts were held by Maratha chiefs (Ajmer by Scindia, 1756–1818), and this is not drawn. Drawn to 1857; the princely-states layer covers 1858 onwards. The Shekhawati chiefs in the north were Jaipur's tributaries and are included; Alwar (independent from 1770) and Tonk (1817) are not.

regions.name: Bikaner State
regions.note: From 1752 the map's Mughal outline no longer covers Rajputana, so the Rajput states, which had been Mughal vassal kingdoms and are drawn inside the Mughal Empire before then, are drawn here as states. Maratha (Scindia, Holkar) armies took tribute and districts until the treaties of 1817–18 put them under British protection. The borders follow the 1909 Rajputana states, which changed little after 1818; before 1818 parts were held by Maratha chiefs (Ajmer by Scindia, 1756–1818), and this is not drawn. Drawn to 1857; the princely-states layer covers 1858 onwards.

regions.name: Kingdom of Jaisalmer
regions.note: From 1752 the map's Mughal outline no longer covers Rajputana, so the Rajput states, which had been Mughal vassal kingdoms and are drawn inside the Mughal Empire before then, are drawn here as states. Maratha (Scindia, Holkar) armies took tribute and districts until the treaties of 1817–18 put them under British protection. The borders follow the 1909 Rajputana states, which changed little after 1818; before 1818 parts were held by Maratha chiefs (Ajmer by Scindia, 1756–1818), and this is not drawn. Drawn to 1857; the princely-states layer covers 1858 onwards. Jaisalmer's desert border with Sindh and Bahawalpur was unsurveyed before the 1840s.

regions.name: Kota State
regions.note: From 1752 the map's Mughal outline no longer covers Rajputana, so the Rajput states, which had been Mughal vassal kingdoms and are drawn inside the Mughal Empire before then, are drawn here as states. Maratha (Scindia, Holkar) armies took tribute and districts until the treaties of 1817–18 put them under British protection. The borders follow the 1909 Rajputana states, which changed little after 1818; before 1818 parts were held by Maratha chiefs (Ajmer by Scindia, 1756–1818), and this is not drawn. Drawn to 1857; the princely-states layer covers 1858 onwards. Zalim Singh, the regent, ruled Kota in practice c. 1771–1824. Jhalawar was split off in 1838 but is kept inside the outline here.

regions.name: Bundi State
regions.note: From 1752 the map's Mughal outline no longer covers Rajputana, so the Rajput states, which had been Mughal vassal kingdoms and are drawn inside the Mughal Empire before then, are drawn here as states. Maratha (Scindia, Holkar) armies took tribute and districts until the treaties of 1817–18 put them under British protection. The borders follow the 1909 Rajputana states, which changed little after 1818; before 1818 parts were held by Maratha chiefs (Ajmer by Scindia, 1756–1818), and this is not drawn. Drawn to 1857; the princely-states layer covers 1858 onwards.

regions.name: Kingdom of Awadh (Oudh), reduced
regions.note: The treaty of 1801 took about half of Awadh (Rohilkhand, the lower Doab and Gorakhpur) for the Company. The map's Cliopatria 'Nawab of Awadh' stops in 1802, although the rest, the Oudh of plate 29 (1837), survived as a protected kingdom until Dalhousie annexed it in February 1856. Its nawabs took the title of king (padshah) from 1819. The northern edge includes the Tarai lands added after the Anglo-Nepalese war (1816).

regions.name: Rohilkhand (Rohilla state)
regions.note: Rohilla Afghan chiefs led by Ali Muhammad Khan made the country between the Ganges and Kumaon (Bareilly, Moradabad, Bijnor, Budaun) a state independent of Delhi by the 1740s. Awadh, helped by Company troops, conquered it in the Rohilla War of 1774, leaving only Rampur to the Rohillas. The map leaves it blank in these years. Najib-ud-Daula's Najibabad (Bijnor) is included, which simplifies matters. It is drawn from 1748 (Ali Muhammad's death and the Durrani-backed restoration); earlier dates are uncertain. Plate 28 shows 'Rohilkhand' in 1765.

regions.name: Kingdom of Kumaon (Chand dynasty)
regions.note: The Chand rajas held Kumaon, from the Kali river to the Garhwal border, and the Tarai below the hills. Gorkha Nepal conquered it in 1790. The map draws these hills inside the Mughal Empire until 1751 and leaves them blank afterwards; the Chands paid occasional tribute but were never under Mughal rule. The southern edge against Rohilkhand and the Tarai is approximate.

regions.name: Garhwal Kingdom
regions.note: The Panwar kings of Garhwal held the upper Ganges and Yamuna hills and Dehradun. Nepal conquered it in 1803–04, and Pradyumna Shah died at Khurbura in 1804. Like Kumaon, the map draws it inside the Mughal outline before 1752 and leaves it blank afterwards.

regions.name: Tehri Garhwal
regions.note: After the Anglo-Nepalese War the Company kept Dehradun and eastern Garhwal and gave the lands west of the Alaknanda back to Sudarshan Shah, who ruled from Tehri. Drawn to 1857; the princely-states layer covers 1858 onwards.

regions.name: Kingdom of Ladakh (Maryul, Namgyal dynasty)
regions.note: The Namgyal kings ruled Ladakh, with Purig, Zanskar and Nubra, from Shey and Leh. They lost Rudok and Guge to Tibet after the war of 1679–84 (Treaty of Tingmosgang), which is not drawn separately. The Dogra general Zorawar Singh conquered Ladakh for Jammu in 1834–41, and the Treaty of Chushul (1842) ended its independence. The map leaves Ladakh blank or draws it inside its neighbours' outlines. Borders in the high, uninhabited north and east are conventional.

regions.name: Kingdom of Sikkim
regions.note: Sikkim's first Chogyals held the hills between the Arun–Tamur rivers (Limbuwan, under looser control) and the Tista. Bhutan took the Kalimpong country east of the Tista in 1706. The Gorkha conquests of the 1770s–80s pushed the western border back to the Mechi and Singalila ridge. The western limit is uncertain.

regions.name: Kingdom of Sikkim
regions.note: Sikkim was confined to the Singalila ridge by the Gorkhas. The Treaty of Titalia (1817) returned the Darjeeling hills taken by Nepal. In 1835 the Chogyal granted Darjeeling to the Company.

regions.name: Kingdom of Sikkim
regions.note: This is Sikkim without the Darjeeling tract, granted in 1835, and without the Morang lowlands annexed by the Company in 1850. Plate 29 (1837, 1857) marks 'Sikkim' here. Drawn to 1857; the princely-states layer covers 1858 onwards.

regions.name: Ahom kingdom (Assam)
regions.note: The Ahom kings held the Brahmaputra valley from Sadiya down to the Bharali–Kallang line, where the Koch kingdom began. Their hold on the hill peoples on both sides varied, and the outline keeps to the valley floor. The map leaves Assam blank in this period.

regions.name: Ahom kingdom (Assam)
regions.note: The Ahom–Mughal wars moved the western frontier back and forth around Guwahati: the Mughals held Kamrup in 1639–67 and 1679–82, and the Ahoms won at Saraighat in 1671. The western edge is drawn at the Barnadi, the frontier agreed in 1639; Guwahati itself changed hands several times.

regions.name: Ahom kingdom (Assam)
regions.note: Gadadhar Singha's victory at Itakhuli (1682) fixed the frontier at the Manas river until the end of the kingdom. The Moamoria rebellion (1769–1805) and the Burmese invasions of 1817–1826 wrecked the state, and the Burmese ruled Assam outright from 1821. The Treaty of Yandabo (1826) gave Assam to the Company. Plate 28 shows 'Assam' in 1765 and 1805.

regions.name: Koch kingdom (Kamata)
regions.note: Under Nara Narayan and his general Chilarai, the Koch kingdom held the land from the Karatoya and Tista to the Bharali river. Its campaigns made Ahom, Manipur, Jaintia, Tripura and the Kachari kingdom tributaries, but those are drawn separately. In 1581 the kingdom split into Koch Bihar and Koch Hajo. The southern edge in Rangpur and Goalpara is approximate.

regions.name: Koch Bihar
regions.note: This is the western half of the Koch kingdom, from the Sankosh to the Tista, with Rangpur district. It was a Mughal vassal from 1609, and Mir Jumla occupied it in 1661–62. It lost Rangpur, Boda and Patgram to the Mughals by 1711.

regions.name: Koch Bihar
regions.note: Koch Bihar was reduced to roughly the later princely state. A treaty of 1773 with the Company, made to expel the Bhutanese, put it under British protection. Plates 28 (1805) and 29 mark 'Cooch Behar'. Drawn to 1857; the princely-states layer covers 1858 onwards.

regions.name: Koch Hajo
regions.note: Koch Hajo was the eastern half of the divided Koch kingdom, from the Sankosh to the Bharali on the north bank, with Goalpara on the south bank. The Mughals conquered it in 1612–13 and the Ahoms and Mughals then fought over it; that contested Kamrup is left blank.

regions.name: Dimasa (Kachari) kingdom
regions.note: After the Ahoms sacked Dimapur (1536) the Dimasa kings ruled the North Cachar hills and the Kopili–Dhansiri uplands from Maibang. The outline is approximate.

regions.name: Dimasa (Kachari) kingdom
regions.note: From the mid-18th century the kings ruled from Khaspur in the Cachar plains (the Barak valley). The Burmese overran it in 1819–24, and the Company annexed the plains in 1832 and the hills in 1834. The date of the move to Khaspur is uncertain (accounts range from the 1690s to the 1750s).

regions.name: Jaintia Kingdom
regions.note: The Syiem Sutnga rajas of Jaintia held the Jaintia hills and the plains below them at Jaintiapur (Sylhet). The Company annexed the plains and then the hills in 1835. The outline is approximate, especially in the plains.

regions.name: Kingdom of Manipur
regions.note: The Meitei kingdom of the Imphal valley and the surrounding hills reached into the Kabaw valley, which Garib Niwaz raided deep into Burma. The Burmese occupied it in 1819–25 ('Seven Years Devastation'). Gambhir Singh won it back with Company help; the Kabaw valley went to Burma in 1834. Drawn to 1857; the princely-states layer covers 1858 onwards.

regions.name: Tripura (Twipra Kingdom)
regions.note: The Manikya kings held the Tripura hills and the plains to the west towards the Meghna (Comilla), contesting Chittagong and Sylhet with Arakan and Bengal. The western plains (Chakla Roshnabad) came under the Mughal Bengal revenue system after 1733.

regions.name: Tripura (Twipra Kingdom)
regions.note: The Manikyas kept 'Hill Tipperah' (marked 'Tipperah' on plates 28–29) as a kingdom. They held the plains estate of Chakla Roshnabad only as zamindars under Bengal and then the Company, so it is left out. Drawn to 1857; the princely-states layer covers 1858 onwards.

regions.name: Khanate of Kalat (Brahui confederacy)
regions.note: The Ahmadzai khans united the Brahui tribes of Sarawan and Jhalawan around Kalat, under Safavid, Mughal and then Afsharid and Durrani overlordship. Nadir Shah gave them Kachhi in 1740. The outline is the Brahui heartland only. Several of the map's outlines (Mughal, Safavid, Afsharid, Durrani) may overlap it.

regions.name: Khanate of Kalat (Nasir Khan's khanate and successors)
regions.note: Nasir Khan I threw off Durrani control (Treaty of Kalat, 1758) and brought Makran, Kharan, Las Bela and Kachhi under the khanate, its greatest extent. It is drawn here with its vassals, while the Durrani outline on the map still includes the region until c. 1820. Gwadar went to Muscat in 1783 (not cut out). The British stormed Kalat in 1839 (Mehrab Khan killed), and the treaty of 1854 made it a British ally. Drawn to 1857; the princely-states layer covers 1858 onwards. The western edge in Makran is approximate.

regions.name: Garha kingdom (Garha-Mandla)
regions.note: At its height under Rani Durgavati, the Gond kingdom of Garha held the upper Narmada valley (Jabalpur, Mandla, Narsinghpur, Damoh and Seoni). She died fighting Akbar's general Asaf Khan in 1564. The map leaves the Gondwana uplands blank until the Maratha outline covers them in 1752. The outline is approximate.

regions.name: Garha-Mandla (Gond kingdom)
regions.note: After 1564 the Gond rajas kept a reduced kingdom around Mandla as Mughal and later Maratha tributaries. The Saugor Marathas annexed it in 1781. From 1752 it lies inside the map's Maratha outline. The map leaves the Gondwana uplands blank until the Maratha outline covers them in 1752.

regions.name: Deogarh (Gond kingdom)
regions.note: The Gond kings of Deogarh held the Chhindwara plateau and the Nagpur plain. Bakht Buland founded Nagpur, and the Bhonsle Raghoji I, called in during a succession dispute, made Burhan Shah a pensioner and founded the Bhonsle kingdom of Nagpur (Wikipedia gives 1739; Raghoji's control is usually dated 1743). The map leaves the Gondwana uplands blank until the Maratha outline covers them in 1752. Dates for the early rulers are uncertain.

regions.name: Chanda (Gond kingdom)
regions.note: The Gond kingdom of Chanda held the Wardha–Wainganga country south of Deogarh. Raghoji I Bhonsle conquered it in 1751. The map leaves the Gondwana uplands blank until the Maratha outline covers them in 1752. The outline is approximate; the southern edge on the Pranhita–Godavari is a convention.

regions.name: Bastar (Kakatiya kingdom)
regions.note: The Kakatiya-descended rajas of Bastar ruled the forested Dandakaranya plateau. They became tributaries of the Bhonsles of Nagpur in the 1770s. The map leaves the Gondwana uplands blank until the Maratha outline covers them in 1752. The outline follows the later Bastar State roughly; the early borders are unknown. After 1751 Bastar is part of the Maratha outline, and from 1818 a Nagpur feudatory (left out of the Nagpur region).

regions.name: Ratanpur (Haihaya kingdom of Chhattisgarh)
regions.note: The Haihaya (Kalachuri) rajas of Ratanpur ruled Chhattisgarh, with a cadet line at Raipur, until the Bhonsle general Bhaskar Pant took Ratanpur in 1741. Wikipedia gives 1758 as the dynasty's final end, under Maratha control. The map leaves the Gondwana uplands blank until the Maratha outline covers them in 1752. The outline is approximate.

regions.name: Bharatpur (Jat kingdom)
regions.note: The Jat state of the Sinsinwars. Under Suraj Mal (1755–63) its power stretched far beyond this outline, over Agra (held 1761–74), Mathura and Mewat; that larger dominion is not drawn. The outline is the later state, which withstood Lake's siege in 1805 and fell to Combermere in 1826. The map's small Mughal outline around Delhi and Agra may overlap its northern part. Drawn to 1857; the princely-states layer covers 1858 onwards.

title: South Asia's regional kingdoms, 1000–1550
summary: Between the Ghaznavid raids and the Mughal conquest, South Asia was shared by dozens of regional states that the border data leaves out: the Madurai Sultanate in the Tamil country, the sultanates of Gujarat, Malwa and Khandesh, the Reddi and Velama kingdoms of Andhra, the Gajapatis of Odisha, the Rajput kingdoms of Mewar and Marwar, the Ahom, Chutia, Kamata and Tripura kingdoms of the north-east, the successors of the Chera Perumals on the Malabar coast, and the Sinhala kingdoms of Gampola, Kotte and Kandy. Their dates and capitals come from cited reference works; their borders are reconstructions checked against Joppen's Historical Atlas of India (1914) and Schwartzberg's Historical Atlas of South Asia. Few medieval sources describe frontiers, so every line here is approximate.

regions.name: Madurai Sultanate (Ma'bar)
regions.note: Proclaimed in 1335 when Jalaluddin Ahsan Khan, Delhi's governor of Ma'bar, threw off Muhammad bin Tughluq's authority; Ibn Battuta visited in 1344. The extent (Vaigai and lower Kaveri down to the Tamirabarani, Ghats crest on the west) follows the old Pandya country and the sultanate's wars with the Hoysala Ballala III, who died besieging its fort near Tiruchirappalli in 1343. The southern limit (Tirunelveli, where Pandya princes survived) and the hold on the Thanjavur delta are uncertain. Dates: Wikipedia 'Madurai Sultanate'; Schwartzberg plate V.2 (Ma'bar 1334–1378).

regions.name: Madurai Sultanate (Ma'bar)
regions.note: Rump sultanate after Vijayanagara's prince Kumara Kampana took Srirangam and the Kaveri country (the Ranganatha image was reinstalled at Srirangam in 1371). Madurai fell and the last sultan was killed in 1378 (Wikipedia 'Madurai Sultanate'). The exact line of the shrinking frontier is not recorded; this slice simply drops the Kaveri belt.

regions.name: Sambuvaraya chiefdom (Tondaimandalam)
regions.note: Former Chola and Pandya vassals who issued records in their own regnal years in the mid-14th century (Wikipedia 'Sambuvarayar'). Kumara Kampana of Vijayanagara defeated Rajanarayana on his march south (Madhura Vijayam); c. 1362 is used here, though some lists run the line to 1375. Extent = northern Tondaimandalam (Palar basin, Ponnaiyar to Pulicat); approximate.

regions.name: Early Vijayanagara (Sangama brothers)
regions.note: Vijayanagara's founding years, before the border data begins (1344). Harihara and Bukka took over the former Kampili kingdom on the Tungabhadra c. 1336; the Hoysala Ballala III still held the south until 1343. Extent = Kampili's lands around Hampi (Schwartzberg V.2 inset e). The 1336 founding date is traditional.

regions.name: Early Bahmani Sultanate
regions.note: The Bahmani state's first years, before the border data begins (1352). Founded by rebel Tughluq officers at Daulatabad in 1347; its four provinces were Gulbarga, Daulatabad, Berar and Bidar (Joppen p. 19; Wikipedia 'Bahmani Sultanate'). The eastern line against the Musunuri Nayakas of Warangal is approximate.

regions.name: Reddi kingdom
regions.note: Founded by Prolaya Vema Reddi after the fall of the Kakatiyas (1323), between the lower Krishna and the Gundlakamma (Wikipedia 'Reddi Kingdom'). Boundaries approximate; Joppen (1398) folds the Reddis into a single 'Telingana'.

regions.name: Reddi kingdom
regions.note: Peak under Anavema and Kumaragiri: from Srisailam to the sea and north to the Godavari delta, where a Rajahmundry branch ruled from the 1390s. Kondavidu fell to Vijayanagara in 1424. Wikipedia 'Reddi Kingdom'; extent approximate.

regions.name: Reddi kingdom of Rajahmundry
regions.note: After Kondavidu fell (1424) the Rajahmundry branch held the Godavari delta until the Gajapati Kapilendra took it c. 1448 (Wikipedia 'Reddi Kingdom').

regions.name: Musunuri Nayakas
regions.note: Telugu chiefs who drove Tughluq forces from Warangal c. 1336; Kapaya ceded Golconda to the Bahmanis (c. 1365) and was overthrown by the Recherla Nayakas in 1368 (Wikipedia 'Musunuri Nayakas'). Extent = Telangana; the western edge facing the Bahmanis moved repeatedly.

regions.name: Recherla Nayakas (Velamas)
regions.note: Padmanayaka Velama chiefs who killed Kapaya Nayaka (1368) and dominated Telangana in the late 14th and early 15th century from Rachakonda and Devarakonda (Wikipedia 'Recherla Nayakas', r. 1375–1435). The Bahmanis took Warangal (1420s) and later the Velama forts; end date approximate.

regions.name: Eastern Ganga Kingdom
regions.note: Last century of the Eastern Gangas (Wikipedia 'Eastern Ganga dynasty'); Firuz Shah Tughluq raided Odisha in 1360. Odisha and northern Kalinga after the border data stops (1351). Western hill limit and southern limit near Simhachalam follow Schwartzberg plate XIV.3(d); approximate.

regions.name: Gajapati Empire
regions.note: Kapilendra Deva seized the throne on the death of the last Ganga king (1434; Wikipedia 'Gajapati Empire'). Odisha and northern Kalinga after the border data stops (1351). Western hill limit and southern limit near Simhachalam follow Schwartzberg plate XIV.3(d); approximate.

regions.name: Gajapati Empire
regions.note: Kapilendra took the Reddi lands: Rajahmundry (c. 1448) and Kondavidu (1454), bringing the frontier to the Krishna (Wikipedia 'Gajapati Empire'). Raids into Telangana and Bahmani territory are not shown as annexations.

regions.name: Gajapati Empire (peak)
regions.note: Prince Hamvira's southern campaign (c. 1463–64) carried Gajapati arms down the Coromandel coast through Udayagiri and Kanchi to the Kaveri; Wikipedia gives the peak as reaching Tiruchirappalli. This was a short military occupation of the coastal belt, lost again by the 1470s; the inland line is a guess.

regions.name: Gajapati Empire
regions.note: During the succession war between Purushottama and Hamvira (who sought Bahmani help, 1471) the Bahmanis took Rajahmundry and Kondavidu; the frontier fell back to about the Godavari.

regions.name: Gajapati Empire
regions.note: Purushottama recovered the coast to the Krishna as the Bahmani state broke up, and the Gajapatis held Udayagiri until Krishnadevaraya took it in 1513. Approximate.

regions.name: Gajapati Empire
regions.note: After Krishnadevaraya's campaigns (Udayagiri 1513, Kondavidu 1515) the 1519 peace left the Gajapatis the land north of the Krishna; Golconda soon pressed on the Godavari districts. Drawn to the Godavari delta. Joppen's 1525 map instead gives the whole coast to Golconda; the mainstream account is followed here.

regions.name: Odisha under the Bhoi dynasty
regions.note: Govinda Vidyadhara usurped the Gajapati throne in 1541; the kingdom kept its core in Odisha (Wikipedia 'Bhoi dynasty'). Same colour as the Gajapatis because it is the same state under a new house. Southern limit approximate.

regions.name: Somavamshi kingdom
regions.note: The Somavamshi (Keshari) kings held Utkala and western Odisha until the Eastern Ganga Anantavarman Chodaganga absorbed Utkala early in the 12th century (Wikipedia 'Somavamshi dynasty', 9th–12th c.). Their Kosala lands went to the Kalachuris; regnal dates are approximate.

regions.name: Kalachuris of Tripuri (Chedi)
regions.note: Core of the Chedi (Dahala-mandala) kingdom on the upper Narmada and Son. Under Lakshmikarna its hegemony briefly reached far beyond; the core is drawn. Joppen p. 14 equates the old kingdom of Chedi with the region south of Bundelkhand; Wikipedia 'Kalachuris of Tripuri'.

regions.name: Kalachuris of Ratnapura
regions.note: Offshoot of the Tripuri Kalachuris in Dakshina Kosala (Chhattisgarh plains), independent from the end of the 11th century (Wikipedia 'Kalachuris of Ratnapura'). Extent = upper Mahanadi plains; approximate.

regions.name: Haihayas of Ratanpur

rulers.name: Pratapamalla
rulers.when: early 13th c., last confirmed of the early line

regions.note: After Pratapamalla the record is thin; a Haihaya dynasty of Ratanpur (with a Raipur branch from about the 14th century) ruled the Chhattisgarh plains until the Marathas (1740s; Wikipedia 'Kalachuris of Ratnapura' gives 1758). Joppen's 1525 map labels the area Chattisgarh within Gondwana. Shown with the same colour; continuity of the line is uncertain.

regions.name: Garha kingdom (Garha-Mandla)
regions.note: Gond kingdom of the upper Narmada, founded in the 15th century (Wikipedia 'Garha kingdom', from 1440). Early extent (Garha-Mandla core) is a guess.

regions.name: Garha kingdom (Garha-Mandla)
regions.note: Sangram Shah enlarged the kingdom to a traditional 52 forts; Joppen's 1525 map marks Jabalpur and Mandla within Gondwana. Extent approximate; dates of Sangram Shah vary between sources.

regions.name: Khandesh Sultanate (Faruqi)
regions.note: Faruqi sultanate of the Tapti valley, often a vassal of Gujarat (Wikipedia 'Farooqui dynasty', 1382–1601; Joppen 1398 map: capital Thalner). Bounded by the Satpuras (Malwa), the Ajanta hills (Bahmani/Ahmadnagar), Berar on the east and Gujarat's Nandurbar district on the west. Continues to 1601 beyond this layer.

regions.name: Tomaras of Gwalior
regions.note: Tughluq feudatories who took Gwalior in the 1390s and kept it against Delhi until Ibrahim Lodi's siege (Wikipedia 'Tomaras of Gwalior', c. 1390–c. 1518). Extent around Gwalior fort; approximate.

regions.name: Malwa Sultanate
regions.note: Dilawar Khan, Tughluq governor, made Malwa independent in 1401; Hoshang Shah moved the capital to Mandu and took Gagron (1423). Wikipedia 'Malwa Sultanate'; extent checked against Joppen's 1398 and 1525 maps (Ujjain, Mandu, Chanderi; Narmada valley to the Satpuras).

regions.name: Malwa Sultanate
regions.note: Peak under Mahmud Khalji I, who fought Gujarat, Mewar and the Bahmanis; eastern districts (Bhilsa, Raisen, Damoh) included as on Joppen's 1525 map. Raids and short occupations (Ajmer, Ranthambore) not shown.

regions.name: Malwa Sultanate
regions.note: After Rana Sanga's victory at Gagron (1519) the north and east (Chanderi under Medini Rai, Raisen and Bhilsa under Silhadi) slipped from the sultan, who kept Mandu, Dhar and Ujjain (Wikipedia 'Malwa Sultanate'). Bahadur Shah of Gujarat annexed Malwa in 1531.

regions.name: Paramara Dynasty
regions.note: Continues the Paramara realm after the border data stops (1235): the dynasty held western Malwa until Alauddin Khalji's conquest in 1305 (Wikipedia 'Paramara dynasty', 948–1305). Reduced extent after Iltutmish's raid on Ujjain (1234–35); approximate.

regions.name: Gujarat Sultanate
regions.note: Zafar Khan (Muzaffar Shah I), Tughluq governor, was effectively independent from the 1390s and took the royal title in 1407 (Wikipedia 'Gujarat Sultanate'; Joppen p. 19). Mainland Gujarat with eastern Saurashtra and the north Konkan ports (Thana, Mahim, contested with the Bahmanis). Champaner, Idar, Junagadh and Kutch were outside or only tributary.

regions.name: Gujarat Sultanate
regions.note: Mahmud Begada annexed Junagadh (1472) and Dwarka (1473), bringing all Saurashtra under the sultanate. Kutch stayed under its Jadeja chiefs; Champaner held out until 1484. Wikipedia 'Gujarat Sultanate'.

regions.name: Gujarat Sultanate
regions.note: Mahmud Begada took Champaner (1484) and made it his capital; the sultanate now held all mainland Gujarat and Saurashtra, as on Joppen's 1525 map.

regions.name: Gujarat Sultanate (with Malwa)
regions.note: Bahadur Shah annexed Malwa (1531) and Raisen (1532) and sacked Chittor (1535) before Humayun overran Gujarat (1535–36). Bassein went to the Portuguese in 1534. The hill country between Gujarat and Malwa (Jhabua, Alirajpur) is bridged over.

regions.name: Gujarat Sultanate
regions.note: Restored after Humayun's withdrawal (1536); Malwa was lost to Mallu Khan (1537), the north Konkan and Diu fort to the Portuguese. The sultanate lasted until Akbar's conquest (1573).

regions.name: Vaghela dynasty (Gujarat)
regions.note: Former Chaulukya generals who took the throne in the mid-1240s and ruled Gujarat until Alauddin Khalji's conquest (1299–1304; Wikipedia 'Vaghela dynasty'). Mainland Gujarat with eastern Saurashtra; the Chudasamas and Kutch chiefs stayed separate.

regions.name: Chudasama kingdom (Sorath)
regions.note: Rulers of Sorath (south-western Saurashtra) with the fortress of Uparkot and Mount Girnar; often tributary to the Chaulukyas and later to Gujarat, conquered by Mahmud Begada in 1472 (Wikipedia 'Chudasama dynasty'). Joppen marks western Kathiawar independent in 1318 and 1398. Extent (Sorath only) approximate; early chronology is mostly bardic.

regions.name: Champaner (Khichi Chauhans)
regions.note: Khichi Chauhan chiefs held the hill fort of Pavagadh and Champaner from about 1300 until Mahmud Begada's 20-month siege (1484), after which Champaner became Gujarat's capital (Wikipedia 'Champaner'; 'Gujarat Sultanate'). Small territory; start date approximate.

regions.name: Kutch (Samma-Jadeja chiefs)
regions.note: Kutch was held by Samma (later Jadeja) chiefs from the 12th century (Wikipedia 'Cutch State', from 1147, capital Lakhiarviro until 1548). Joppen shows Kutch independent in 1318 and 1398. It was divided among branches until Khengarji I united it; its Rann and Wagad edges are approximate.

regions.name: Kingdom of Mewar (Guhilas)
regions.capital: Nagda and Aghata (Ahar); Chittor in the 13th c.
regions.note: The Guhilas of Medapata, sovereign from the 10th century and fighting Paramaras, Chaulukyas and Chahamanas (Wikipedia 'Guhila dynasty'). Chittor fell to Alauddin Khalji in 1303. Core Mewar between the Aravallis and the Banas; approximate.

regions.name: Kingdom of Mewar (Sisodias)
regions.note: Hammir Singh of the Sisodia branch recovered Chittor (1326) and refounded the kingdom (Wikipedia 'Kingdom of Mewar'). Approximate.

regions.name: Kingdom of Mewar
regions.note: Rana Kumbha built Kumbhalgarh, took Mandalgarh and fought Malwa and Gujarat; Marwar was under Mewar control 1438–1453. Approximate.

regions.name: Kingdom of Mewar (Rana Sanga)
regions.note: Rana Sanga's hegemony: Ranthambore and the Hadoti country, victory over Malwa at Gagron (1519) with Chanderi and Raisen held by his vassals (not drawn). Ended by Babur's victory at Khanwa (1527). Extent approximate.

regions.name: Kingdom of Mewar
regions.note: After Khanwa Mewar fell back to its core; Bahadur Shah of Gujarat sacked Chittor in 1535 and Sher Shah received its submission in 1544. Approximate.

regions.name: Kingdom of Marwar (Mandore)
regions.note: The Rathores, at Pali since the 13th century, moved to Mandore under Rao Chunda in 1395 (Wikipedia 'Kingdom of Marwar'). After Rao Ranmal's murder at Chittor (1438) Mewar held Mandore until Jodha retook it (1453). Approximate.

regions.name: Kingdom of Marwar
regions.note: Rao Jodha recovered Mandore (1453) and founded Jodhpur (1459); kinsmen founded Bikaner and Merta. Approximate.

regions.name: Kingdom of Marwar (Maldeo)
regions.note: Rao Maldeo took Nagaur, Ajmer, Merta, Jalore and Sambhar and briefly Bikaner (1542), until Sher Shah's victory at Sammel (1544). Wikipedia 'Kingdom of Marwar'. Bikaner's occupation is not drawn. Approximate.

regions.name: Kingdom of Marwar
regions.note: Maldeo recovered Jodhpur after Sher Shah's death (1545); drawn at its core extent. Approximate.

regions.name: Bikaner kingdom
regions.note: Rao Bika, a son of Rao Jodha, conquered the Jat clans of Jangladesh from 1465 (Wikipedia 'Bikaner State'). Maldeo of Marwar held it 1542–44 (not shown). Continues as a princely state. Approximate.

regions.name: Kingdom of Jaisalmer
regions.note: Rawal Jaisal moved the Bhati capital from Lodhruva to Jaisalmer in 1156 (Wikipedia 'Kingdom of Jaisalmer'); the desert kingdom was sacked by Delhi's forces c. 1299 but survived. Borders in the Thar are notional.

regions.name: Chahamanas of Jalor
regions.note: Branch of the Naddula Chahamanas, Chaulukya feudatories and then independent, ended by Alauddin Khalji's siege of Jalore (1311; Wikipedia 'Chahamanas of Jalor'). Joppen's 1398 map marks Jalor. Approximate.

regions.name: Chahamanas of Ranthambore
regions.note: Founded by Prithviraja III's son Govindaraja as a Ghurid vassal in 1192, alternately subject to and independent of Delhi, ended by Alauddin Khalji's siege (1301; Wikipedia 'Chahamanas of Ranastambhapura'). Approximate.

regions.name: Emirate of Multan
regions.note: Isma'ili emirate of Multan, conquered by Mahmud of Ghazni in 1010 (Wikipedia 'Emirate of Multan', 855–1010). Extent approximate.

regions.name: Soomra dynasty (Lower Sindh)
regions.note: Local dynasty of Lower Sindh, tributary at times to the Ghaznavids, Qabacha and Delhi (Wikipedia 'Soomra dynasty', 1026–1351). Drawn to 1343 because the border data shows the Samma state from 1344; the Samma takeover (1335–1351) is gradual. King lists are largely traditional.

regions.name: Qabacha's sultanate (Multan and Uch)
regions.note: Muhammad of Ghor's governor of Multan made himself independent after 1206 and held Upper Sindh and Multan until Iltutmish took Uch (1228). Lower Sindh's Soomras paid him tribute and are drawn separately. Extent approximate.

regions.name: Langah Sultanate
regions.note: Sultanate of the lower Punjab doab around Multan and Uch; annexed by the Arghuns in 1528 (Wikipedia 'Langah Sultanate'). Joppen's 1525 map shows 'Multan' as a strip along the Sutlej and Indus. Approximate.

regions.name: Arghun dynasty (Sindh)
regions.note: Shah Beg Arghun, driven from Kandahar by Babur, took Thatta from the Sammas (c. 1520); his son conquered Multan (1528, not drawn) (Wikipedia 'Arghun dynasty'). The border data keeps the Samma state to 1525. Approximate.

regions.name: Khasa Malla kingdom
regions.note: Himalayan kingdom of the Karnali basin with its capital at Sinja, which at times also ruled Purang and Guge; it broke up into the Baise principalities in the late 14th century (Wikipedia 'Khasa Kingdom'). Schwartzberg V.2 marks the Mallas here. Hill extent only; approximate.

regions.name: Guge kingdom
regions.note: Western Tibetan kingdom of the upper Sutlej, at times holding Spiti, Kinnaur and Zanskar (Wikipedia 'Guge'); its line was interrupted in the 12th–14th centuries when Khasa Malla kings held sway. Continues to 1630. Extent approximate.

regions.name: Kingdom of Maryul (Ladakh)
regions.note: Westernmost Tibetan kingdom, from the Zoji La to Demchok with Rudok (Wikipedia 'Kingdom of Maryul', c. 930–1842). Extent approximate.

regions.name: Karnats of Mithila (Tirhut)
regions.note: Dynasty of Mithila (Tirhut) founded by Nanyadeva in 1097, ended when Ghiyath ad-Din Tughluq took Tirhut (1324) (Wikipedia 'Karnats of Mithila'; Schwartzberg V.2). Between the Gandak and the Kosi; approximate.

regions.name: Sonargaon Sultanate
regions.note: East Bengal broke from Delhi under Fakhruddin Mubarak Shah (1338), who also took Chittagong; Ilyas Shah annexed it in 1352 (Joppen p. 19: Bengal independent 1340; Wikipedia 'Bengal Sultanate'). Western line along the Jamuna-Padma; approximate.

regions.name: Sultanate of Lakhnauti (Ilyas Shah)
regions.note: West and north Bengal (Lakhnauti and Satgaon) before Ilyas Shah united Bengal in 1352; shares the Bengal Sultanate's colour because Ilyas Shah founded it. The border data's tiny 1344–51 polygon is left in place. Approximate.

regions.name: Kamata kingdom
regions.note: Successor of western Kamarupa after Sandhya moved his seat to Kamatapur sometime after 1257 (Wikipedia 'Kamata Kingdom'); conquered by Alauddin Husain Shah of Bengal in 1498. Goalpara, Kamrup, Cooch Behar, Jalpaiguri and Rangpur; eastern limit approximate.

regions.name: Koch kingdom
regions.note: Biswa Singha rebuilt the former Kamata kingdom after Bengal's rule there collapsed (Wikipedia 'Koch dynasty', from 1515). Same frame as Kamata; approximate.

regions.name: Ahom kingdom
regions.note: Sukaphaa's small Tai principality on the south bank of the upper Brahmaputra (Wikipedia 'Ahom kingdom', 1228–1826). Approximate.

regions.name: Ahom kingdom
regions.note: Gradual growth down the south bank and against the Kacharis. Approximate.

regions.name: Ahom kingdom
regions.note: Suhungmung annexed the Chutia kingdom (1523–24) and pushed west to Kaliabor while repelling Bengal's invasions. Approximate.

regions.name: Ahom kingdom
regions.note: The Ahoms sacked the Dimasa capital Dimapur (1536) and took the Dhansiri valley. Approximate.

regions.name: Chutia kingdom
regions.note: North-bank kingdom around Sadiya (Lakhimpur, Dhemaji, Tinsukia and the Arunachal foothills), believed founded in the 13th century and prominent from the 14th; annexed by the Ahoms in 1523–24 (Wikipedia 'Chutia kingdom'). Start date approximate.

regions.name: Dimasa (Kachari) kingdom
regions.note: Kachari kingdom of the Dhansiri valley and North Cachar hills, one of the states that grew out of Kamarupa (Wikipedia 'Dimasa Kingdom'). Its founding date is unknown; Ahom chronicles place Kacharis here from the 13th century. Few rulers before the 16th century are securely dated.

regions.name: Dimasa (Kachari) kingdom
regions.note: After the Ahoms sacked Dimapur (1536) the Dimasa capital moved to Maibang in the North Cachar hills. Approximate.

regions.name: Twipra (Tripura) kingdom
regions.note: Manikya kingdom of the Tripuri people, established by Maha Manikya c. 1400 (Wikipedia 'Twipra Kingdom'). Hill core; approximate.

regions.name: Twipra (Tripura) kingdom
regions.note: Dhanya Manikya and his successors pushed into the Comilla plains and contested Chittagong with Bengal and Arakan (Chittagong not drawn). Approximate.

regions.name: Manipur (Kangleipak)
regions.note: Meitei kingdom of the Imphal valley (Wikipedia 'Manipur (princely state)', kingdom from 1110). The surrounding hills are included only roughly. Continues as a princely state.

regions.name: Chera Perumal kingdom (Mahodayapuram)
regions.note: The medieval Chera kingdom, from the Chandragiri river to Nagercoil at its height (Wikipedia 'Chera Perumals of Kerala', c. 844–c. 1124); Chola invasions in the early 11th century did not end it. Its break-up c. 1124 produced Venad, Kolathunadu, Calicut and Cochin. Approximate.

regions.name: Venad (Kingdom of Quilon)
regions.note: Southernmost successor of the Chera Perumals: Kollam, Thiruvananthapuram and Nanjinad (Wikipedia 'Venadu kingdom'). The northern limit against Kayamkulam and the Ghats line are approximate; Ravi Varma's campaign to Kanchi (1312–13) is not drawn.

regions.name: Kolathunadu (Cannanore)
regions.note: North Malabar between the Chandragiri and Korapuzha rivers (Wikipedia 'Kolathunadu'). Inland limit approximate.

regions.name: Calicut (Zamorin's kingdom)

rulers.name: Samoothiri (dynastic title)
rulers.when: Ibn Battuta at Calicut, 1342; Vasco da Gama, 1498

regions.note: The Samoothiri of Nediyiruppu Swaroopam made Calicut the chief port of the Malabar coast (Wikipedia 'Zamorin'). It was flourishing when Ibn Battuta came in 1342; its start date is uncertain (c. 1300 used). Extent between the Korapuzha and Ponnani with Eranad; approximate.

regions.name: Kingdom of Cochin (Perumpadappu Swaroopam)
regions.note: Perumpadappu Swaroopam became a free principality after the Chera Perumals fell in the 12th century and rose to importance with the Portuguese (Wikipedia 'Kingdom of Cochin'). Extent around Kodungallur and Kochi; approximate, and much smaller before 1500.

regions.name: Kingdom of Gampola
regions.note: Sinhala kingdom of the south-west and centre, with the Alagakkonara ministers dominant at Kotte late in the century (Wikipedia 'Kingdom of Gampola', 1341–1408). The Jaffna kingdom and the Vanni chiefs held the north. Approximate.

regions.name: Kingdom of Kotte
regions.note: Parakramabahu VI moved the capital to Kotte (1412) (Wikipedia 'Kingdom of Kotte'). Approximate.

regions.name: Kingdom of Kotte (whole island)
regions.note: Prince Sapumal conquered the Jaffna kingdom (c. 1450) and the Vanni was brought under Kotte, uniting the island until Parakramabahu VI's death (1467) (Wikipedia 'Kingdom of Kotte').

regions.name: Kingdom of Kotte
regions.note: Jaffna regained independence and the hill country broke away as Kandy (c. 1469). Approximate.

regions.name: Kingdom of Kotte
regions.note: After the 'Spoiling of Vijayabahu' (1521) Kotte kept the western coast around Colombo and leaned on the Portuguese. Approximate.

regions.name: Kingdom of Kandy
regions.note: Hill-country kingdom founded in the late 15th century (Wikipedia 'Kingdom of Kandy', 1469–1815), with influence over the east coast. Approximate.

regions.name: Kingdom of Sitawaka
regions.note: Mayadunne's share of the 1521 partition of Kotte, which absorbed Raigama in 1538 (Raigama not drawn separately) (Wikipedia 'Kingdom of Sitawaka'). Approximate.

sites.name: Vijayanagara (Hampi)
sites.what: capital founded by the Sangama brothers, c. 1336

sites.name: Kondavidu
sites.what: Reddi capital; taken by Vijayanagara 1424, Gajapatis 1454

sites.name: Dhar
sites.what: Paramara capital; first Malwa sultanate capital

sites.name: Anhilwad Patan
sites.what: first Gujarat sultanate capital; old Chaulukya capital

sites.name: Multan
sites.what: seat of the emirate and the Langah sultanate

sources.title: C. Joppen, Historical Atlas of India (1914), maps 10–14: India in 1022, 1236, 1318, 1398, 1525 (archive.org)

title: Tamilakam in the Sangam age
summary: Sangam poetry (the Purananuru, Akananuru, Ten Idylls and Patirruppattu) describes a Tamil country running from the Venkatam hills to Cape Kumari. It was shared by three 'crowned kings' and a ring of Velir chiefs in the hills between them. The Cholas held the Kaveri delta, the Pandyas the Vaigai and Tamirabarani basins, and the Cheras the Malabar coast and later Kongu. Ashoka's edicts, the Hathigumpha inscription, the Periplus, Pliny, Ptolemy, Tamil-Brahmi inscriptions and digs at Keezhadi, Kodumanal, Arikamedu and Pattanam confirm the kingdoms, capitals and ports. No source draws a frontier, though: these borders are inferred from where named places, rivers and hills cluster, and they are approximate. The changes over time follow Nilakanta Sastri's dating, which puts most named kings in c. 100–250 CE. Other scholars place them a century or more earlier.

regions.name: Chola kingdom (Chola Nadu)

rulers.name: Karikal Valavan (Karikala)
rulers.when: c. 1st–2nd century CE (disputed; Sastri c. 190 CE)

rulers.name: Killivalavan
rulers.when: after Karikala; attacked Madurai and Vanji (Kanakasabhai); date unknown

regions.capital: Uraiyur (Ptolemy's 'Orthoura'); port and later seat Kaveripattinam (Puhar)
ports: Kaveripattinam (Puhar; Ptolemy's Khaberis, probably the Periplus' Camara)
regions.attested: Ashoka RE II and XIII ('Cholas'); Pattinappalai and Porunararruppadai (Karikala's battles of Venni and Vahaipparandalai); Purananuru; Ptolemy
regions.note: The core of the kingdom is the Kaveri delta and Uraiyur. The western edge near Kulithalai, where Kongu begins, and the northern edge on the Vellar river are conventions taken from later Chola geography. The southern frontier with the Pudukkottai chiefs is not described anywhere. Karikala's victories gave the Cholas leadership over the other kings, but the poems do not show any permanent annexation beyond the delta.

regions.name: Aruva Nadu (lower Pennai valley)
ports: Arikamedu (Poduke of the Periplus and Ptolemy, probably)
regions.attested: Pattinappalai (the Aruvalar); Ptolemy's 'Aruvarnoi' (as read by Kanakasabhai); Arikamedu excavations (Wheeler 1945; Begley 1989–92)
regions.note: Sastri places the Aruvalar's country in the lower Pennai valley, north of the Kaveri delta. Kanakasabhai uses Aruva Nadu more widely, for the whole country around Kanchi, so this region is grouped with Tondai Nadu. Its southern edge on the Vellar and its northern edge near Marakkanam are approximate.

regions.name: Aruva Nadu under Chola overlordship
regions.attested: Pattinappalai: 'the ancient Aruvalar carried out his behests' (as summarised by Sastri)
regions.note: The poem records the Aruvalar submitting to Karikala, not being annexed. The change is dated to c. 190 CE only because that is Sastri's date for Karikala; other scholars place Karikala anywhere from the 1st century BCE to the 2nd century CE.

regions.name: Tondai Nadu (Kanchi and the Tiraiyar)

rulers.name: Tondaiman Ilandiraiyan of the Tiraiyar line

ports: Sopatma of the Periplus (location uncertain; Kanakasabhai's Eyil-pattinam)
regions.attested: Perumbanarruppadai (on Ilandiraiyan); Tolkappiyam preface and Akananuru (Venkatam as the northern limit, beyond it the Vadugar); Ptolemy's Malanga (Kanchi, per Kanakasabhai)
regions.note: The northern line follows the Venkatam (Tirupati) hills, with Pulicat on the coast. These are the limits given by the Tolkappiyam preface, which is a later addition to the text, and by medieval commentators. Sastri finds no sign that Ilandiraiyan was subject to the Cholas. The claim that Karikala settled Tondai rests on a medieval document. The Pallavas held Kanchi by the late 3rd century.

regions.name: Malaiyaman Nadu (Kari of Kovalur)

rulers.name: Kannan, son of Kari
rulers.when: later a minister of the Cholas (Kanakasabhai)

regions.capital: Kovalur (Tirukkoyilur) on the Pennai; hill fort of Mullur
regions.attested: Purananuru (Kapilar's songs on Kari); Akananuru 208 (Kari kills Ori); Jambai Tamil-Brahmi inscription of Adiyaman Anji, near Tirukkoyilur (1st century CE)
regions.note: This region covers the middle Pennai valley between the Chola delta and Tondai Nadu. Kanakasabhai treats the Malaiyaman as a Chola vassal: when Kari took the crown, the Cholas invaded. Adiyaman also stormed Kovalur, and his inscription at Jambai shows how much the chiefs' territories overlapped.

regions.name: Nannan of Chenkanma (Cheyyar valley)

rulers.name: Nannan, son of Nannan
rulers.when: patron of the Malaipadukadam (c. 2nd–3rd century CE)

regions.capital: Chenkanma (Chengam), in the valley of the Cheyyar
regions.attested: Malaipadukadam of Perunkausikanar (Kanakasabhai's reading)
regions.note: This is a different chief from Nannan of Ezhimalai. Kanakasabhai places him in the Chengam valley of the Cheyyar. Others put the Malaipadukadam's Nannan in Tondai Nadu, which is the same general area. The boundary is a rough box around the Javadi hills and the Chengam pass.

regions.name: Adiyaman chiefdom (Tagadur)

rulers.name: Adiyaman Neduman Anji
rulers.when: 1st century CE by the Jambai inscription; c. 190 CE on Sastri's chronology

regions.attested: Ashoka RE II 'Satiyaputa' (equated with the Adiyaman by Burrow and Sastri); Jambai inscription 'Satiyaputo Atiyan Neduman Anji'; Purananuru (Auvaiyar's songs on Anji)
regions.note: The heartland is the Dharmapuri plateau, between the Kaveri gorge and the Javadi hills. The Jambai inscription gives Anji the title 'Satiyaputa', which strongly supports identifying Ashoka's Satiyaputras with the Adiyaman line. Some still doubt the inscription; R. Nagaswamy defended it.

regions.name: Tagadur under Chera suzerainty
regions.attested: Patirruppattu (Arisil Kilar's decad on Perunjeral Irumporai, who took Tagadur); the lost Tagadur Yattirai
regions.note: After Tagadur fell, the Adiyaman acknowledged Chera overlordship and died fighting Nannan at Pali on the Cheras' behalf (Sastri). The date of the change depends on Sastri's chronology, and the inscriptions may point earlier.

regions.name: Kongu Nadu (Kosar and local chiefs)
regions.capital: Kodumanal (industrial centre, not a known capital)
regions.attested: Sangam poems on the Kosar of Kongu (Sastri); Kodumanal excavations (bead-making and iron working, c. 5th–1st century BCE); Roman coin finds around Karur and Coimbatore
regions.note: Kongu is the upper Kaveri, Bhavani, Noyyal and Amaravati country, roughly the Salem and Coimbatore districts. It lies between the Nilgiris, the Palghat gap and the Kolli hills. No early dynasty is attested here. The Kosar, once thought to be Ashoka's Satiyaputras, are linked to Kongu in the poems.

regions.name: Kongu under the Irumporai Cheras (Karuvur)

rulers.name: Ko Atan Cheral Irumporai, Perunkadungon, Ilankadungo
rulers.when: three generations named at Pugalur (c. 2nd century CE)

regions.capital: Karuvur (Karur) on the Amaravati, identified as Vanji by Sastri
regions.attested: Pugalur Tamil-Brahmi inscriptions (Mahadevan 2003); Patirruppattu (Irumporai decads); Ptolemy's 'Karoura, royal seat of Kerobothros'
regions.note: Sastri credits 'Kuttuvan of many elephants' with conquering Kongu, so the change is placed c. 150 CE. The Pugalur inscriptions, dated 1st–2nd century CE, could put it earlier. Whether Vanji, the Chera capital, was Karur or a site in Kerala is still debated.

regions.name: Kolli hills (Ori)
regions.attested: Akananuru 208; Kapilar's songs (Sastri)
regions.note: This is the Kolli massif itself. The chiefdom ended when Malaiyaman Kari killed Ori.

regions.name: Kolli hills under the Cheras
regions.attested: Kapilar via Sastri: Kari 'transferred his mountain, Kollimalai, to the Cheras'; Patirruppattu titles
regions.note: The date is set between Kapilar's floruit and Irumporai's reign on Sastri's chronology, and is approximate.

regions.name: Pekan of the Avi clan (Palani hills)

rulers.name: Pekan (Vel Avi family)
rulers.when: patron visited by Sangam bards (Kanakasabhai); date unknown

regions.attested: Purananuru (songs on Pekan); Tirumurugarruppadai (Avinankudi)
regions.note: Identifying Pekan's country with Palani rests on tradition, linking Avinankudi and Pothini with Palani. The sources consulted support this only weakly. The boundary is drawn around the Palani hills.

regions.name: Irukkuvel chiefdom (Kodumbalur)
regions.attested: Pattinappalai; Purananuru (Kapilar offers Pari's daughters to Irungovel)
regions.note: This is the Pudukkottai buffer between the Cholas and Pandyas. It is not certain that the Sangam Irungovel is the same as the later Irukkuvels of Kodumbalur, and some scholars place him further north-west.

regions.name: Parambu (Pari)

rulers.name: Vel Pari
rulers.when: contemporary of Kapilar; killed when the three kings besieged Parambu

regions.attested: Purananuru c. 105–120 (Kapilar's songs and the lament of Pari's daughters)
regions.note: Sastri places Parambu at Piranmalai, in the Pandya country. The poems give it 300 villages around a fortified hill. The boundary is a small notional area.

regions.name: Parambu after Pari's fall
regions.attested: Purananuru (siege by the three crowned kings)
regions.note: All three kings besieged Parambu, and no source says who kept it. It is assigned to the Pandyas only because Piranmalai lies in Pandya country.

regions.name: Pandya kingdom (Pandya Nadu)
regions.capital: Madurai (Kudal); Korkai, the pearl port where the heir apparent lived
regions.attested: Ashoka RE II and XIII ('Pandyas'); Hathigumpha inscription of Kharavela (pearls from the Pandya); Maduraikkanchi; Pliny ('Pandion' at Madura); Periplus (Colchi, Nelcynda); Ptolemy
regions.note: The core is the Vaigai and Tamirabarani basins, bounded on the west by the crest of the Ghats at Podiyil. The northern line, against Palani, Kongu and the Pudukkottai chiefs, is a guess. Nedunjeliyan's annexation of the Milalai and Mutturu districts (Sastri) is not drawn.

regions.name: Kuttanad (attribution unknown)
regions.attested: Kanakasabhai counts Kuttanad among the five Chera nadus (based on later sources)
regions.note: No early evidence names the ruler of the backwater coast south of Muziris. It is shaded Chera only by default.

regions.name: Nelcynda coast under the Pandyas
regions.attested: Periplus 54 ('Nelcynda ... of another kingdom, the Pandian'); Pliny NH 6.26 (Becare, of the Neacyndi, king Pandion at Madura)
regions.note: Both 1st-century Roman sources put the pepper port of Nelcynda under the Pandyas, across the Ghats from Madurai. Where exactly Nelcynda was is disputed.

regions.name: Kuttanad in the country of the Aioi
regions.attested: Ptolemy, Geography VII.1 (Melkynda listed in the country of the Aioi; as quoted by Kanakasabhai)
regions.note: By Ptolemy's time, Nelcynda (his 'Melkynda') lies in the Ay country. This may be a real change or just a different source. The exact frontier with the Cheras is unknown.

regions.name: Ay chiefdom (Podiyil and Nanjil Nadu)

rulers.name: Ay Andiran
rulers.when: patron of the poet of Uraiyur (Sastri)

regions.capital: Aykudi (site uncertain), around the Podiyil hill
regions.attested: Purananuru 127–136 (Ay); 137–140 (Nanjil Nadu); Ptolemy's 'Aioi', with Cape Komaria and Mount Bettigo
regions.note: This region covers the southern end of the Ghats and the coast to Kanyakumari, including Porunan's Nanjil Nadu. The Periplus instead puts the coast from Comari eastward under the Pandyas, so the line near the cape is contested.

regions.name: Chera kingdom (Kuda Nadu, Malabar coast)
regions.capital: Vanji: Tiruvanchikulam near Kodungallur, Tiru-Karur on the Periyar (Kanakasabhai), or Karur in Kongu (Sastri) — disputed
regions.attested: Ashoka RE II ('Kelalaputa'); Patirruppattu; Akananuru 149 (Yavana ships at Muziris); Periplus 54 (Tyndis and Muziris in the kingdom of Cerobothra); Pliny (Muziris, king Coelobothras)
regions.note: Sastri and Gurukkal see two Chera lines: one on the coast, and the Irumporai at Karur. The northern limit at Badagara follows the Periplus' White Island, as Kanakasabhai reads it. The eastern limit is the Ghats crest, with the Palghat gap included. Pattanam's link to Muziris is strong but not certain.

regions.name: Nannan of Ezhimalai (Pali)

rulers.name: Nannan (title borne by several rulers)
rulers.when: killed by Narmudicheral (Patirruppattu 40); his general killed Adiyaman Anji at Pali

regions.capital: Pali, on the slopes of Ezhimalai (Ezhil hill)
regions.attested: Akananuru 152, 199, 396; Natrinai 270; Patirruppattu 40 and 4th decad; Sastri ('north of Malabar, in the Tulu country')
regions.note: This is the north-western edge of Tamilakam, from Badagara to about Kasaragod and inland to Coorg. Sources disagree on which Nannan ruled which lands, and the Kosar of Chellur also raided Ezhimalai.

sites.name: Keezhadi
sites.what: urban settlement on the Vaigai near Madurai; the excavator's report claims 8th c. BCE–3rd c. CE, and the ASI (2025) asked for justification of the pre-5th-century-BCE phase (contested)

sites.name: Madurai
sites.what: Pandya capital (Kudal), described in the Maduraikkanchi

sites.name: Korkai
sites.what: Pandya pearl-fishing port at the Tamirabarani mouth (Ptolemy's Kolkhoi); now inland

sites.name: Uraiyur
sites.what: early Chola capital on the Kaveri (Ptolemy's Orthoura)

sites.name: Kaveripattinam (Puhar)
sites.what: Chola port at the Kaveri mouth, subject of the Pattinappalai

sites.name: Arikamedu
sites.what: Indo-Roman trading port, probably Poduke; Wheeler (1945) dated it to the late 1st c. BCE–2nd c. CE, Begley (1989–92) to the 2nd c. BCE onward

sites.name: Venkatam (Tirupati hills)
sites.what: traditional northern limit of Tamilakam (Tolkappiyam preface)

sites.name: Tirukkoyilur and Jambai
sites.what: Kovalur, seat of Malaiyaman Kari; nearby Jambai has the 1st-century CE inscription of 'Satiyaputo' Adiyaman Anji

sites.name: Tagadur (Dharmapuri)
sites.what: seat of the Adiyaman chiefs, taken by Perunjeral Irumporai

sites.name: Karur and Pugalur
sites.what: Karuvur, the Irumporai Cheras' seat (possibly Vanji); Pugalur Tamil-Brahmi inscriptions naming three Chera generations (c. 2nd c. CE)

sites.name: Kodumanal
sites.what: bead-making and iron-working centre on the Noyyal, c. 5th–1st c. BCE (uncalibrated dates, debated)

sites.name: Pattanam (Muziris?)
sites.what: probable site of Muziris; Roman amphorae of the 1st c. BCE–1st c. CE, earlier habitation

sites.name: Ezhimalai
sites.what: hill of Nannan's chiefdom; Pali lay on its slopes
